A real-Docker test of `verifyEvidenceComplete` rejecting a container that exited normally (not via the timeout/signal path) but with genuinely corrupted evidence (e.g. an OOM-killed candidate mid-run) — covered instead by direct unit tests against hand-crafted incomplete/missing artifact files (fast, deterministic, and exercises the exact same gate) plus the real-Docker timeout case, which is the realistic way this gate is reached in practice.
judgment_calls: Test scenarios are a closed, code-owned registry (`tool_test_scenarios.ts`, shared with D1.3's validator) of 3 fixed, non-sensitive CLI invocations (`--version`, `--help`, no-args) — a `tool-install` proposal selects 2 or 3 of these BY IDENTIFIER, never by prompt text. This keeps the track's no-raw-prompts invariant structural (there is no field capable of carrying prompt text at all) while still genuinely invoking the installed candidate, closing the D1.2 repair's Blocker B gap.

Each scenario's stdout/stderr is redirected into a transient, on-disk (bind-mounted, host-side-but-scratch) log purely for the SAME network/credential-signature scanning the install step already used, then discarded with the rest of the scratch directory — never returned, never logged, never persisted raw.

Forbidden-path violations are detected via pre-seeded sentinel files with a known content hash, checked for a content/hash change (or disappearance) after the run — verified by hand to work under the container's user (a permission-bit/chmod-000 approach was considered and rejected: even a non-root process that OWNS a file it wrote can still corrupt it, so hash comparison is the only reliable signal regardless of container user).

Credential ACCESS attempts (reads, not writes) are counted by how many times a sentinel's marker text appears in the captured install+invocation output — a `cat`/read prints the sentinel's content, which the run script redirects into logs this module parses for a COUNT ONLY; the raw log content itself is discarded and never returned or persisted.

Teardown correctness (`docker kill` + `docker rm -f` in a `finally`, not relying on `--rm` alone, targeting only the exact generated name) was verified BY HAND against this environment before being encoded: killing the `docker run` CLI client process (e.g. on a timeout) does NOT stop the container — `--rm` only fires on the CONTAINER's own exit, not its client's.

Install methods are a closed, explicit set (`npm install`, `pip install`, plus a TEST-ONLY `local-script` escape hatch never accepted by the production proposal validator in D1.3) — an unrecognised installMethod fails closed to `verdict: 'unknown', reason: 'unsupported_install_method'` rather than guessing at a shell invocation.

The container now runs as the `node:22-alpine` image's built-in non-root `node` user with a read-only root filesystem; the bind-mounted `/vet` scratch workspace is chmod 0o777 on the host side specifically so a non-root, non-host-uid-mapped container user can still create/modify files there regardless of which uid created the directory — verified against the real local Docker daemon by the full real-Docker suite passing unchanged with these flags applied.

The live Docker tests use `node:22-alpine` (already present locally in this environment, confirmed via `docker images` before writing any code) specifically to avoid any image-pull network dependency in the test suite; `--pull never` is also passed on every real `docker run` so a missing image fails fast and deterministically rather than the vetting infrastructure itself silently reaching the internet.

The 'network calls observed' detection is a closed set of known DNS/connection-failure error signatures (`getaddrinfo`, `Could not resolve host`, `failed to connect`, `ENETUNREACH`, `ECONNREFUSED`) parsed out of captured install+invocation output under `--network none`; a network-capable ecosystem tool not covered by one of these signatures would under-report rather than over-report — ponytail: extend the signature list if a real generator surfaces one this misses.

The test suite's scratch root is now created under `os.tmpdir()` (guaranteed to exist on every platform) rather than a hardcoded absolute path assumed to pre-exist, and is torn down only via its own tracked path in `afterAll` — never a sweep of anything else under the OS tmp directory.
